hook: I wrapped $34 worth of ribbon wrong for 3 years

scenes.visual_prompt: A tree with ribbon wrapped in a tight single helix, looking like a candy cane
scenes.voiceover: For three years I wrapped ribbon in one tight helix. It always came out looking like a candy cane.

scenes.visual_prompt: Diagram overlay showing diagonal spiral starting points offset by roughly 30 degrees between each wrap
scenes.voiceover: The fix is offsetting where each spiral starts by about 30 degrees from the one above it.

scenes.visual_prompt: Close-up of ribbon with a pre-attached floral wire being twisted around a branch to secure it
scenes.voiceover: Start at the top third, run it diagonally down, and secure it to a branch every 12 to 18 inches with the wire that's already attached to the ribbon.

scenes.visual_prompt: Side-by-side of wired satin ribbon fraying and catching light vs. velvet ribbon with a clean cut edge
scenes.voiceover: Velvet doesn't fray at a cut edge, so there's no finishing. Wired satin catches light at every hard point and needs the wire reshaped at every loop.

scenes.visual_prompt: Hands counting out 3-4 full spirals top to base on a 7.5-foot tree
scenes.voiceover: Three to four full spirals cover a 7.5-foot tree. Two is plenty for anything 5 feet or under.

scenes.visual_prompt: Finished tree with evenly offset diagonal ribbon, no candy-cane pattern visible
scenes.voiceover: Same ribbon, same tree, completely different result.

caption: I've been wrapping ribbon wrong since I started decorating my own tree. The spiral technique that actually avoids the candy-cane look, plus the wire-securing math nobody tells you — full breakdown on the blog.
